demographics: Men are more likely to use most illicit drugs and to have drug use disorders; women progress from first use to dependence more quickly and are more likely to present in primary care or emergency settings
Highest prevalence of illicit drug use is in adults ages 18–25
Non-Hispanic American Indian or Alaska Native and multiracial adults have the highest rates of substance use disorder; Asian adults have the lowest
Sexual and gender minority youth and adults have higher rates of substance use than the general population
Lower household income and less education are associated with higher rates of drug-related harm

risk_factors.text: Family history of substance use disorder
Untreated mental health condition such as depression, anxiety, PTSD, or ADHD
Initiation of drug use in adolescence
Peer or social network that uses drugs
Adverse childhood experiences, including abuse, neglect, or household substance use
Easy access to prescription opioids, benzodiazepines, or stimulants, including a personal or household prescription

family_history: Substance use disorder in a parent or sibling
social_history: Lives with or spends most time with people who use drugs
Trouble at school, work, or in relationships
Loss of job, housing, or custody
Recent release from jail or prison
Sex work or exchange of sex for drugs or money
exposures: Club drugs such as MDMA or GHB
Over-the-counter medications used to get high, such as dextromethorphan or loperamide

chief_complaints.text: I just can't stop using, even though it's ruining my life
I've been feeling awful and shaky since I tried to cut back
My family says I have a problem and made me come in
I need something for my pain, my usual pills ran out early
I've been sleeping terribly and my mood is all over the place
I overdosed last week and woke up in the ER

hpi.onset: Usually begins in adolescence or early adulthood, often with a first exposure at a party, from a friend, or through a prescription after an injury; escalation to a problem pattern typically builds over months to years
hpi.duration: Weeks to decades; most patients describe a pattern lasting at least a year by the time they seek care
hpi.progression: Use becomes more frequent and in larger amounts than intended; the person spends more time obtaining, using, and recovering; tolerance develops so more is needed for the same effect; withdrawal appears when use stops; use continues despite clear harm to health, work, money, and relationships
hpi.quality: The patient describes a loss of control over use, strong craving, and preoccupation with the drug that crowds out other interests
hpi.severity: Varies; patients often describe it as moderate to severe and worse during withdrawal or after a recent overdose
hpi.timing: Often daily or several times a day; some use in binges separated by days of crash and recovery
aggravating: Being in places linked to past use
relieving: Being in treatment or a structured program
Support from family or a recovery group
Stopping contact with people who use

associated_symptoms.text: Needing more of the drug to get the same effect
Withdrawal symptoms when cutting down or stopping
Neglecting work, school, or family duties
Sleep problems, either too little or too much
Spending more money than planned on the drug
Seizures during withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines

atypical.how_it_differs: Often begins with a prescribed opioid, benzodiazepine, or sedative after surgery or for chronic pain; patients may underreport use, present with falls, confusion, or worsening chronic disease rather than a request for help, and are more sensitive to sedation and withdrawal.

Patients often hide use because of fear of child protective services; presentation may be late or no prenatal care, and withdrawal in the newborn after delivery is a common first sign. Opioid use in pregnancy is treated with methadone or buprenorphine rather than abrupt withdrawal.
Adolescents may present with declining grades, truancy, new peer group, mood swings, or an overdose; younger children present after accidental ingestion of a household medication or an adult's drug.
missing_classic_features: Self-reported craving or loss of control

atypical.how_it_differs: Injection drug use with immune suppression raises the risk of unusual infections such as invasive fungal infections and atypical pneumonia, so fever and focal findings may dominate the picture.

criteria.name: Substance use disorder
criteria.summary: A problematic pattern of use leading to impairment or distress, with at least two of the following in a 12-month period: taking more or for longer than intended; wanting to cut down or unsuccessful attempts; spending a lot of time obtaining, using, or recovering; craving; failure to meet obligations; continued use despite social problems; giving up activities; use in hazardous situations; continued use despite physical or psychological harm; tolerance; withdrawal. Severity is mild (2–3), moderate (4–5), or severe (6 or more).

differential.name: Opioid intoxication or overdose
differential.why_considered: Altered mental status, sedation, and respiratory depression in a patient who uses drugs
differential.trigger: Pinpoint pupils with slow, shallow breathing or unresponsiveness

history: Recent use of heroin, fentanyl, or prescription opioids
Found down with drug paraphernalia nearby
Known opioid use disorder
labs: Hypercapnia with respiratory acidosis on blood gas
Opioids or fentanyl on urine drug screen
imaging: Chest x-ray may show aspiration or pulmonary edema

differential.name: Alcohol withdrawal and delirium tremens
differential.why_considered: Tremor, agitation, autonomic hyperactivity, and seizures in a patient who uses substances
differential.trigger: Tremor, sweating, and tachycardia hours to days after last drink

history: Heavy daily alcohol use
Last drink 6–48 hours ago
Prior withdrawal seizures
exam: Disorientation and hallucinations in severe cases

differential.name: Benzodiazepine withdrawal
differential.why_considered: Anxiety, tremor, insomnia, and seizures after stopping sedatives
differential.trigger: Seizure or severe anxiety after abruptly stopping a prescribed or illicit benzodiazepine

history: Long-term benzodiazepine use
Abrupt dose reduction or running out of pills
Prior withdrawal seizure

differential.name: Major depressive disorder
differential.why_considered: Low mood, anhedonia, sleep and appetite change, and poor function

history: Depressed mood most of the day for at least two weeks
Anhedonia
Symptoms present during periods of abstinence

differential.name: Generalized anxiety disorder
differential.why_considered: Restlessness, irritability, poor concentration, and sleep problems

Symptoms not tied to intoxication or withdrawal

differential.name: Post-traumatic stress disorder
differential.why_considered: Avoidance, hyperarousal, nightmares, and substance use as self-medication

Avoidance of reminders

differential.why_considered: Confusion, agitation, tremor, and diaphoresis that mimic intoxication or withdrawal
differential.trigger: Altered mental status with sweating and tremor; check a bedside glucose

Missed meal
Symptoms relieved by eating

differential.why_considered: Chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea after cocaine or methamphetamine use

differential.why_considered: Agitation, tremor, clonus, and hyperthermia in a patient taking serotonergic drugs
differential.trigger: Clonus and hyperthermia after starting or combining serotonergic agents

differential.why_considered: Rigidity, fever, and altered mental status in a patient taking antipsychotics
differential.trigger: Lead-pipe rigidity with high fever and autonomic instability after an antipsychotic

history: Recent antipsychotic start or dose increase
Recent discontinuation of a dopaminergic drug

differential.name: Malingering or secondary gain
differential.why_considered: Requests for controlled substances or exaggerated symptoms for external benefit

history: Request for a specific controlled drug
Symptoms that shift with observers
Legal or financial incentive
exam: No objective signs of intoxication or withdrawal
labs: Toxicology negative for the drug the patient claims to use

severity.mild: Two to three criteria for a substance use disorder met; use continues despite some harm but most obligations are met; no physiologic dependence or withdrawal
severity.moderate: Four to five criteria met; clear loss of control, craving, and role impairment; tolerance or withdrawal may be present; still able to engage in treatment
severity.severe: Six or more criteria met; daily or binge use, physiologic dependence with withdrawal, major health, legal, and social consequences, and repeated failed attempts to stop
severity.critical: Life-threatening presentation: opioid overdose with respiratory depression, severe alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal with seizures or delirium, stimulant-induced myocardial infarction or hyperthermia, or sepsis from injection-related infection

red_flags.finding: Chest pain with ST changes after stimulant use

red_flags.meaning: Serotonin syndrome or neuroleptic malignant syndrome; a medical emergency

red_flags.finding: Active suicidal ideation with a plan
red_flags.meaning: High risk of self-harm; requires immediate psychiatric evaluation

red_flags.finding: Hypotension with tachycardia and elevated lactate

clues: Last drink or benzodiazepine 6–72 hours ago

complications.name: Skin and soft tissue infection or abscess
Blood-borne infections such as HIV and hepatitis C

complications.name: Stimulant-induced myocardial infarction or arrhythmia

special_populations.differences: Opioid use disorder is treated with methadone or buprenorphine rather than abrupt withdrawal; untreated withdrawal risks fetal loss. Newborns may show withdrawal after delivery, and patients often avoid care because of fear of child protective services.

Use often starts with a prescribed opioid, benzodiazepine, or sedative after surgery or for chronic pain; patients may present with falls, confusion, or worsening chronic disease rather than a request for help and are more sensitive to sedation and withdrawal.

Adolescents may present with declining grades, truancy, a new peer group, mood swings, or an overdose; younger children present after accidental ingestion of a household medication or an adult's drug.
Liver disease changes drug metabolism and raises the risk of toxicity; many medications used for addiction treatment need dose adjustment, and coagulopathy increases bleeding risk.

Reduced clearance raises the risk of drug accumulation and toxicity; some medications used for opioid use disorder need dose adjustment, and rhabdomyolysis is more likely to cause acute kidney injury.
Injection drug use with immune suppression raises the risk of unusual infections such as invasive fungal infections and atypical pneumonia, so fever and focal findings may dominate the picture.

key_questions.question: Tell me about your drug use — what do you use, how much, and how often?
key_questions.looking_for: Specific substances, route (oral, snorting, smoking, injection), amount, and frequency; ask about each class separately

key_questions.question: When did you last use, and what happens when you stop or cut back?
key_questions.looking_for: Timing of last use and withdrawal symptoms; determines risk of seizures or delirium

key_questions.question: Have you ever tried to cut down or stop? What happened?
key_questions.looking_for: Unsuccessful attempts to quit or control use — a core feature of a substance use disorder

key_questions.question: Do you need more of the drug than you used to for the same effect?
key_questions.looking_for: Tolerance

key_questions.question: Do you ever use more than you planned, or for longer than you meant to?
key_questions.looking_for: Loss of control over amount or duration of use

key_questions.question: How much of your day goes to getting, using, or recovering from the drug?
key_questions.looking_for: Time spent obtaining, using, and recovering; craving and preoccupation

key_questions.question: Has your use caused problems at work, school, or home, or with people close to you?
key_questions.looking_for: Failure to meet obligations and continued use despite social or interpersonal problems

key_questions.question: Have you given up activities or hobbies you used to enjoy?
key_questions.looking_for: Giving up important social, occupational, or recreational activities

key_questions.question: Have you used in situations where it was physically dangerous, like driving or operating machinery?
key_questions.looking_for: Use in hazardous situations

key_questions.question: Have you kept using even though you knew it was hurting your health or your mind?
key_questions.looking_for: Continued use despite physical or psychological harm

key_questions.question: Have you ever overdosed or woken up in an emergency room after using?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior overdose — a strong marker of severe disorder and high risk of another

key_questions.question: Do you inject? Do you ever share needles, syringes, or other equipment?
key_questions.looking_for: Injection use and sharing — drives risk of HIV, hepatitis B and C, and endocarditis

key_questions.question: How do you get the drug, and how do you pay for it?
key_questions.looking_for: Prescription sources, illicit supply, sex work or selling drugs, financial strain

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have a problem with drugs or alcohol?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of substance use disorder — a strong risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you been feeling depressed, anxious, or unable to sleep? Any thoughts of hurting yourself?
key_questions.looking_for: Co-occurring depression, anxiety, PTSD, or ADHD and any suicidal ideation

key_questions.question: Have you ever heard voices or felt paranoid or watched when you were using or coming down?
key_questions.looking_for: Stimulant-induced paranoia or hallucinations; whether psychosis clears with abstinence

key_questions.question: Are you taking any prescribed medicines, especially opioids, benzodiazepines, or stimulants?
key_questions.looking_for: Prescribed controlled substances, who prescribes them, and whether they are taken as directed

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy changes treatment entirely; opioid use disorder in pregnancy is treated with methadone or buprenorphine, not withdrawal

key_questions.question: Where are you living now, and who do you spend most of your time with?
key_questions.looking_for: Unstable housing, incarceration, or a social network that uses drugs

key_questions.question: Any fevers, chills, or sores where you inject?
key_questions.looking_for: Skin infection, abscess, or systemic infection such as endocarditis

reasoning_points: A problematic pattern of use causing impairment or distress, with at least two features in a 12-month period
Features include using more or longer than intended, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, craving, and time spent obtaining or recovering
Continued use despite physical, psychological, or social harm, and giving up important activities
Tolerance and withdrawal indicate physiologic dependence and raise severity
Severity is graded by the number of features: mild (2–3), moderate (4–5), severe (6 or more)
Route of use matters: injection raises risk of HIV, hepatitis B and C, skin infection, and endocarditis
Screen for co-occurring depression, anxiety, PTSD, ADHD, and suicide risk
Assess for withdrawal risk, especially alcohol and benzodiazepines, which can cause seizures or delirium
Pregnancy must be checked because it changes the entire treatment plan

easy: Young adult with a clear story of escalating use, craving, and loss of control
Obvious consequences such as job loss, arrest, or relationship breakdown
Physical signs such as track marks or pinpoint pupils
Patient openly reports the drug and pattern of use
medium: Patient minimizes use or presents with a physical complaint such as an abscess or chest pain
Co-occurring depression or anxiety that masks the substance problem
Prescription opioid use that started legitimately after surgery or injury
Withdrawal symptoms that bring the patient in without a stated drug history
hard: Older adult started on a prescribed opioid or benzodiazepine who presents with falls or confusion
Pregnant patient who hides use for fear of child protective services
Adolescent with declining grades and mood swings but no self-reported use
Stimulant-induced psychosis that must be distinguished from a primary psychotic disorder
Patient with a normal exam and normal labs who is seeking controlled substances
